display.name: Jules Park
display.blurb: A 31-year-old investor with a written rulebook: position caps, a borrowing line, a premium to pay, an approval trap, an exploit and a rebalancing day.

intro: Jules Park, 31, a professional who is curious about crypto and already invests. Take-home pay $3,700 a month. Living costs $2,800 a month. Opening: checking $1,200, emergency reserve $5,600, index fund $20,000, retirement account $30,000, so the investment base starts at $50,000. No DeFi, no debt. All figures in this scenario are assumptions for the exercise.
plan: 5% per position: no single DeFi position above 5% of the investment base.
10% in total: all DeFi positions together stay at or under 10% of the base.

Caps are tested before each purchase, against the base as it stands when he decides, counting the full purchase amount (fee included). Exactly at a cap is allowed. A position can drift above 5% as prices rise; that is not a purchase breach, but he cannot add to it.
Rebalancing trigger: 8% of the base, measured on total DeFi (Harbor Vault + Surge Pool + ETH).
Cash for bills, not borrowing or selling, when checking already covers the bill. The $5,600 reserve is the last resort.
Investment base = index fund + retirement account + DeFi positions, at market value. Checking, the reserve and loans are not in it.

questions.title: The vote, and the permission
questions.situation: Surge Pool has a governance proposal: "Proposal 14: change how the pool's treasury is held." A dashboard offers two ways to take part. Voting costs about $8 in network gas and uses a one-time signature for this vote only. A convenience button asks you to approve unlimited spending of your pool tokens "so future votes and claims are one click." No financial effect from the vote is modeled.

b.t: Read the proposal and vote with a one-time signature. $8 gas from checking. No spending permission is granted.

unavail.label: Unavailable: you hold no pool tokens, so you have no vote.

c.t: Click "approve unlimited spending" to make future voting easier.

It scores 0 because the approval lets a contract move all of your current and future pool tokens with no limit or expiry, and you cannot tell in advance whether that contract will always behave. In this story, a month later the approved spender was abused and 25% of your pool position ({-lt.d.POOL}) was drained. The drain shows the risk; it is not the reason for the score. Next: a smaller pool position, and the approval is still open until you revoke it.
c.ref: You approved unlimited spending. It scores 0 because the approval lets a contract move all of your current and future pool tokens with no limit or expiry, and you cannot tell in advance whether that contract will always behave. In this story, a month later the approved spender was abused and **25% of your pool position ($263.02) was drained**. The drain shows the risk; it is not the reason for the score. Next: a smaller pool position, and the approval is still open until you revoke it.

questions.takeaway: Approving a spender is a permission, not a vote. Prefer one-time signatures and exact amounts. Review and revoke approvals you no longer need. Governance power is worth using only if you have read what you are voting on.
